examTakeaway: ADH inserts aquaporins in the collecting duct, so urine concentrates only when that hormone is present.
scenario: A 36-year-old woman has a pituitary mass removed. The next day urine output is 300 mL/h and urine osmolality is 80 mOsm/kg. Serum sodium is 150 mEq/L. After a dose of desmopressin the urine osmolality rises to 500. She is not on lithium.
question: Which channel appeared in the collecting duct after the dose?
options: The urea transporter of the liver
explanation: ADH inserts aquaporins in the collecting duct, so urine concentrates only when that hormone is present. Aquaporin-2 is the channel desmopressin inserts, which is why the urine then concentrates. ENaC reabsorbs sodium under aldosterone and does not concentrate the urine by itself. NKCC2 is the loop transporter blocked by furosemide. The urea transporter of the liver is not what a desmopressin dose inserts in the kidney. A sodium-glucose cotransporter is an SGLT drug target in the proximal tubule.

examTakeaway: Aldosterone adds sodium channels in the collecting duct and secretes potassium, so volume rises and potassium falls.
scenario: A 50-year-old man has a blood pressure of 160/96 mm Hg and a potassium of 3.1 mEq/L. He is not on a diuretic. Plasma renin is low. An adrenal vein sample on the left is hormone-rich compared with the right. He asks what the excess hormone does to the collecting-duct cell.
question: Which pair of effects does that hormone have?
options: Hydrogen secretion only, with no potassium change
Calcium reabsorption in the proximal tubule
explanation: Aldosterone adds sodium channels in the collecting duct and secretes potassium, so volume rises and potassium falls. Sodium retention and potassium secretion is that pair. Sodium loss and potassium retention is the opposite pattern. Water channels without sodium change describes ADH. Calcium reabsorption in the proximal tubule is not the aldosterone effect. Hydrogen secretion only, with no potassium change, misses the potassium wasting that brought him in.

examTakeaway: Parathyroid hormone raises calcium by bone resorption, kidney reabsorption, and activation of vitamin D.
scenario: A 58-year-old woman has a calcium of 11.6 mg/dL, a low phosphate, and a PTH that is high rather than suppressed. She has no lung mass and PTHrP is undetectable. She asks which three actions the high PTH is using to raise the calcium.
question: Which set of actions raises the calcium?
options: Bone resorption, kidney reabsorption, and vitamin D activation
Kidney calcium wasting and a high phosphate
Calcitonin release from the thyroid C cells
correctAnswer: Bone resorption, kidney reabsorption, and vitamin D activation
explanation: Parathyroid hormone raises calcium by bone resorption, kidney reabsorption, and activation of vitamin D. Bone resorption, kidney reabsorption, and vitamin D activation is that set, and phosphate falls because the kidney dumps it. Bone formation only would lower calcium. Kidney calcium wasting and a high phosphate is the opposite of PTH. Suppression of vitamin D would lower calcium. Calcitonin release from the thyroid C cells lowers calcium.

examTakeaway: PTHrP from a lung cancer raises calcium and suppresses PTH, which is how it differs from a parathyroid adenoma.
scenario: A 64-year-old man with a new lung mass has a calcium of 12.4 mg/dL. PTH is suppressed. PTHrP is high. Phosphate is low. He has no neck mass. He asks why the parathyroid hormone itself is low if the calcium is high.
question: Why is PTH low while calcium is high?
options: The kidney is making extra PTH
A tumor peptide mimics PTH and the real gland shuts off
Calcitonin is the hormone that is high
correctAnswer: A tumor peptide mimics PTH and the real gland shuts off
explanation: PTHrP from a lung cancer raises calcium and suppresses PTH, which is how it differs from a parathyroid adenoma. A tumor peptide mimics PTH and the real gland shuts off, so measured PTH is low. The parathyroids are oversecreting would show a high PTH. Vitamin D is absent would lower calcium. Calcitonin is the hormone that is high would lower calcium. The kidney is making extra PTH is not a renal product.

examTakeaway: Insulin moves GLUT4 into muscle and fat membranes, so those tissues take up glucose only after insulin arrives.
scenario: A 17-year-old boy with new type 1 diabetes has a glucose of 420 mg/dL and large urine ketones. He has not yet received insulin. Muscle biopsy research in similar patients shows the glucose transporter still sitting in intracellular vesicles. He asks what insulin does to that transporter.
question: What does insulin do to the muscle glucose transporter?
options: It opens a potassium channel in the muscle
It moves GLUT4 to the cell surface
It inserts GLUT2 in the muscle
It blocks SGLT2 in the kidney as its main action
correctAnswer: It moves GLUT4 to the cell surface
explanation: Insulin moves GLUT4 into muscle and fat membranes, so those tissues take up glucose only after insulin arrives. It moves GLUT4 to the cell surface. It inserts GLUT2 in the muscle is wrong; GLUT2 is the liver and beta-cell transporter and is not insulin-dependent. It blocks SGLT2 in the kidney as its main action is a drug class, not insulin. It opens a potassium channel in the muscle is not the glucose-uptake step. It destroys glucose is not a mechanism.

examTakeaway: Cortisol raises blood glucose by permitting gluconeogenesis, which is why a low cortisol can present as hypoglycemia.
scenario: A 30-year-old man on long-term prednisone stops it abruptly. Two days later glucose is 48 mg/dL, blood pressure is 86/50 mm Hg, and he is weak. He is not septic. ACTH is low because the pituitary axis is suppressed. He asks why stopping the steroid dropped the glucose.
question: Which hepatic pathway lost its permit when the steroid stopped?
options: Glycogen storage as the only pathway
explanation: Cortisol raises blood glucose by permitting gluconeogenesis, which is why a low cortisol can present as hypoglycemia. Gluconeogenesis is the pathway that lost its cortisol permit. Glycogen storage as the only pathway would not explain a glucose of 48 after the stores are gone. Ketone use by the brain does not require cortisol. Insulin secretion would lower glucose if it rose, and here the problem is missing cortisol. GLUT4 insertion is an insulin effect in muscle, not the missing hepatic permit.

examTakeaway: Thyroid peroxidase organifies iodide, so a block there causes a high TSH and a large gland that cannot make hormone.
scenario: A 14-year-old girl has a growing goiter, fatigue, and a TSH of 40 mIU/L. Free T4 is low. A radioiodine scan shows the gland takes up iodide but does not organify it; perchlorate then discharges the iodide. She is not taking thyroid hormone.
question: Which enzyme failed to attach iodine to thyroglobulin?
explanation: Thyroid peroxidase organifies iodide, so a block there causes a high TSH and a large gland that cannot make hormone. Thyroid peroxidase is the enzyme the perchlorate discharge test shows has failed. 5-prime deiodinase converts T4 to T3 in peripheral tissues and would not trap iodide in the gland. Aromatase makes estrogen. 21-hydroxylase is an adrenal enzyme. Tyrosine hydroxylase makes catecholamines.

examTakeaway: Growth hormone acts on the liver to make IGF-1, so a liver failure can cause poor growth even when the pituitary is normal.
scenario: A 10-year-old boy with cirrhosis has fallen off his growth curve. Growth hormone is high. IGF-1 is low. The pituitary is normal on MRI. Bone age is delayed. He asks why a high growth hormone is not making him grow.
question: Which organ failed to answer the growth hormone?
explanation: Growth hormone acts on the liver to make IGF-1, so a liver failure can cause poor growth even when the pituitary is normal. The liver is the organ that should have made IGF-1 and did not. The adrenal makes cortisol, not IGF-1. The thyroid makes T4. The pancreas makes insulin. The gonad makes sex steroids. None of those is the missing IGF-1 step.

examTakeaway: Prolactin is held down by dopamine, so a drug that blocks dopamine receptors can cause galactorrhea.
scenario: A 29-year-old woman starts risperidone. Two months later she has galactorrhea and amenorrhea. Prolactin is 80 ng/mL. TSH is normal. MRI shows no pituitary mass. She asks how an antipsychotic raised the prolactin.
question: Which brake did the drug remove?
explanation: Prolactin is held down by dopamine, so a drug that blocks dopamine receptors can cause galactorrhea. Dopamine inhibition of the lactotroph is the brake risperidone removed. TRH from a failing thyroid would raise TSH, which is normal, and there is no mass. Somatostatin from the hypothalamus inhibits growth hormone more than this picture. Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary ejects milk but does not raise prolactin to 80. Cortisol negative feedback is the adrenal axis.

examTakeaway: Estrogen closes the epiphyseal plate, which is why an early puberty shortens adult height.
scenario: A 7-year-old girl has had breast development for a year and a growth spurt. Bone age is 11 years. LH rises after GnRH stimulation. Her predicted adult height is now shorter than the mid-parental height. She asks why growing fast now means ending up shorter.
question: Which hormone is closing the growth plates early?
explanation: Estrogen closes the epiphyseal plate, which is why an early puberty shortens adult height. Estrogen from the early puberty advances bone age and then fuses the plates. Growth hormone excess would enlarge hands later, not fuse plates at age 7. Cortisol excess stunts growth without a pubertal LH rise. Insulin does not close plates. Thyroxine deficiency delays bone age, the opposite of an age of 11.

examTakeaway: Progesterone raises the set point for temperature, which is why the basal temperature rises after ovulation.
scenario: A 26-year-old woman charts a basal temperature that jumps 0.4 C and stays up for 12 days, then falls when bleeding starts. An LH surge was detected the day before the rise. She is not ill. She asks which hormone raised the temperature set point.
question: Which hormone raised the temperature set point?
explanation: Progesterone raises the set point for temperature, which is why the basal temperature rises after ovulation. Progesterone from the corpus luteum is the hormone that holds the temperature up until bleeding. Estrogen in the follicular phase is high before the LH surge, when the temperature is still low. FSH recruits the follicle and does not set temperature. Prolactin and oxytocin are not the luteal temperature signal.
